title: Level 2 – International Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Mother and Newborn Care
intro: Supporting Mothers and Newborns Student learning Notes Welcome to GNPS Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse. International maternity settings expect nurses to combine evidence-based assessment with cultural safety, structured escalation, multidisciplinary teamwork and informed family participation. This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations. It strengthens your ability to interpret fetal and maternal trends, manage high-risk pregnancy, respond to obstetric and neonatal emergencies and communicate clearly across maternity and neonatal teams. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Apply international standards for maternal and newborn assessment Interpret fetal wellbeing and labour-progress information Recognise and escalate high-risk pregnancy complications Respond to common obstetric emergencies Manage postpartum deterioration and maternal mental-health concerns Assess and stabilise high-risk newborns Provide culturally safe and trauma-informed maternity care Coordinate care across multidisciplinary teams Support informed choice, education and safe discharge International practice requires more than following routines. Nurses must integrate the woman's history, current observations, fetal wellbeing, labour progress, newborn adaptation and family preferences while remaining alert to rapid deterioration. By completing Level 2, you should be able to deliver safe, culturally responsive and evidence-informed maternity and newborn care while meeting the professional expectations of international healthcare environments.

content.text: International maternity practice places strong emphasis on early risk identification, evidence-based monitoring and shared decision-making. High-risk pregnancy may involve hypertension, diabetes, placental problems, infection, fetal growth concerns or preterm labour.
Learning outcomes
Assess women with high-risk pregnancy conditions Interpret maternal and fetal trends
Recognise preeclampsia, diabetes and placental complications Escalate concerns using structured communication

Hypertensive Disorders Preeclampsia may present with hypertension, proteinuria, headache, visual disturbance, upper abdominal pain or abnormal laboratory results. Severe disease can progress to seizures, stroke or organ dysfunction.
Gestational Diabetes Nursing care includes glucose monitoring, medication or insulin support, nutrition education and surveillance for maternal and fetal complications.

Placental Complications Placenta previa may cause painless bleeding, while placental abruption often causes pain, uterine tenderness and bleeding. Vaginal examination may be unsafe until placental location is known.
Preterm Labour and Fetal Growth Regular contractions, cervical change, leaking fluid or pressure before term require prompt evaluation. Reduced fetal growth or movement also requires assessment.

A woman at 35 weeks reports severe upper abdominal pain and visual disturbance. Her blood pressure is markedly elevated. The nurse recognises severe preeclampsia, initiates urgent escalation, prepares prescribed treatment and monitors maternal and fetal status closely.
Key learning points
Treat severe hypertension symptoms as urgent Do not perform unsafe procedures when placenta previa is possible
Monitor mother and fetus together Use structured escalation and clear documentation

Obstetric emergencies can develop suddenly and threaten the life of the mother, fetus or both. Effective nursing response requires rapid assessment, role clarity, teamwork and preparation for emergency birth or resuscitation.
Learning outcomes
Recognise common obstetric emergencies Prioritise immediate maternal and fetal actions
Work effectively within emergency teams Provide clear communication and emotional support

Postpartum Haemorrhage Rapid blood loss requires immediate activation of the emergency response, uterine assessment, medication and fluid support as prescribed, preparation for blood products and ongoing monitoring.
Cord Prolapse and Fetal Compromise Cord prolapse can reduce fetal oxygenation. Immediate pressure relief, maternal positioning, emergency assistance and preparation for urgent birth are required.
Shoulder Dystocia and Uterine Rupture These emergencies require immediate team response and adherence to established manoeuvres or surgical pathways.
Amniotic Fluid Embolism and Collapse Sudden hypoxia, hypotension or collapse requires resuscitation, emergency obstetric and critical-care support and rapid coordination.

After rupture of membranes, the fetal heart rate falls sharply and the nurse sees the umbilical cord at the vaginal opening. The nurse calls for emergency assistance, relieves pressure on the cord according to protocol, positions the woman and prepares for immediate operative birth.
Key learning points
Activate help early Use established emergency protocols
Protect maternal and fetal oxygenation Communicate clearly during rapidly changing events

High-risk newborns may be premature, growth restricted, hypoglycaemic, jaundiced, infected or experiencing respiratory distress. Their condition can deteriorate quickly, making close assessment and timely intervention essential.
Learning outcomes
Assess a high-risk newborn systematically Recognise respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia and sepsis
Support thermoregulation, feeding and oxygenation Communicate effectively with neonatal teams and families

Prematurity and Low Birth Weight Premature newborns are vulnerable to heat loss, respiratory difficulty, infection, feeding problems and unstable blood glucose. Developmentally supportive care is important.
Respiratory Distress Grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, central cyanosis or apnoea require immediate assessment and neonatal support.
Hypoglycaemia and Jaundice At-risk newborns require appropriate monitoring. Treatment may include feeding support, glucose therapy or phototherapy according to severity and policy.
Neonatal Sepsis Temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, respiratory change or abnormal colour may indicate infection. Early escalation and treatment are essential.

A premature newborn develops grunting, chest retractions and falling oxygen saturation. The nurse maintains warmth, supports the airway, applies prescribed respiratory support and urgently involves the neonatal team while informing the parents calmly.
Key learning points
Subtle newborn changes may be significant Maintain warmth and glucose stability
Escalate respiratory distress immediately Include parents in care whenever clinically possible

Maternity care occurs within personal, cultural and family contexts. International nurses must communicate respectfully, support informed choice and avoid assumptions about pregnancy, birth, feeding or family roles.
Learning outcomes
Provide culturally safe maternity and newborn care Support informed choice and shared decision-making
Use interpreters and accessible communication Provide trauma-informed and compassionate support
Cultural Safety Nurses should ask what matters to the woman and family rather than assuming preferences based on background. Cultural practices should be accommodated when safe.
Informed Choice Women should receive clear information about options, benefits, risks and alternatives and have time to ask questions. Consent is an ongoing process.
Communication Access Professional interpreters should be used for complex or high-risk discussions. Information should also be adapted for literacy, hearing, vision or cognitive needs.

Trauma, Loss and Bereavement Pregnancy loss, emergency birth and neonatal illness can be traumatic. Compassionate communication, privacy, memory-making where appropriate and referral to support services are important.

A woman with limited English requires an urgent caesarean birth. The nurse arranges an interpreter, explains what is happening in clear steps, checks understanding and keeps the chosen support person involved where possible. Urgency does not remove the need for respectful communication.
Key learning points
Ask rather than assume preferences Use professional interpreters for complex information
Support informed participation even during urgent care Provide compassionate care after trauma or loss

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 6 - Level 2, you have strengthened your ability to manage high-risk pregnancy, respond to obstetric emergencies, care for vulnerable newborns and provide culturally safe family-centred care. You are now prepared for Level 3, where the focus moves to leadership, quality improvement and global maternal-newborn health.
